e.etymology: A modern American name, a Jah- spelling of Jamari, which blends the Ja- prefix with names like Amari and Jamar. The spelling echoes Jah, the Rastafari name for God.
A Danish name, a medieval Latinized short form of names beginning with the Germanic element wig or vig, 'battle', Old Norse vig. It spread to Norway and Sweden in the 19th century.
namesakes: Viggo Mortensen (Aragorn in The Lord of the Rings)

assoc.t: Viggo Mortensen, The Lord of the Rings actor

e.etymology: A spelling of Jaylin or Jaelyn, a modern American blend of Jay and the -lyn ending. This form is used mostly in Hispanic families.
From Greek doron, 'gift', and theos, 'god', the same elements as Theodora in reverse order. Dorothy is the everyday English form; Dorothea is the older Latinate one, borne by an early saint.
namesakes: Dorothea Dix (19th-century reformer of mental health care)
Dorothea Lange (Depression-era photographer of Migrant Mother)
Dorothea Brooke (heroine of George Eliot's Middlemarch)

assoc.t: dorothea, Taylor Swift song from the album evermore

e.meaning: unknown; the wife of Aeneas in Roman legend
e.etymology: A Latin name of obscure meaning, tied to the ancient town of Lavinium. In Virgil's Aeneid, Lavinia is the Latin princess who marries Aeneas. English speakers have used it since the 17th century.
namesakes: Lavinia (Titus's daughter in Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus)

e.etymology: From Sanskrit ananya, 'having no other, unique', formed from an-, 'not', and anya, 'other'. One of the most popular girls' names in India in recent decades.
A modern American spelling with more than one source: a form of Kali or Cali for girls, and a short form of Khalil for boys.

assoc.t: The Great Khali, towering WWE wrestler

e.note: In Hindi, Urdu and Persian, khali means empty.

e.etymology: Feminine of Junius, a Roman family name probably linked to the goddess Juno; older sources read it as 'youth'. In Romans 16:7 Paul greets Junia as outstanding among the apostles.
A modern American name that joins Ace to the -lynn ending, in the pattern of Gracelynn and Raelynn.
A spelling of Azariah, from Hebrew Azaryah, 'Yahweh has helped', borne by many men in the Old Testament. In the US this spelling is now given mostly to girls.
From the English word quest, which comes through Old French queste from Latin quaerere, 'to seek'. It is also a German surname, but American parents use it as a word name.

assoc.t: A Tribe Called Quest, hip-hop group

e.etymology: From a surname that is a variant of Irvine or Irving, a Scottish place name probably meaning green or fresh water, or of Irwin, from Old English eofor, 'boar', and wine, 'friend'.
From an English surname for a maker or seller of cord, from Old French cordel, 'small rope'.
namesakes: Cordell Hull (FDR's secretary of state and Nobel Peace laureate)
Cordell Walker (Chuck Norris's hero in Walker, Texas Ranger)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Oved, 'serving, worshipping'. In the Book of Ruth, Obed is the son of Ruth and Boaz and the grandfather of King David.
A spelling of Muhammad, from Arabic hamida, 'to praise', the name of the Prophet of Islam and one of the most common names in the world. The -ed spelling follows Turkish usage.

assoc.t: the Prophet Muhammad, founder of Islam

e.etymology: The original Hebrew form of Joshua, 'Yahweh is salvation', the name of Moses's successor who led Israel into Canaan. Its shortened form Yeshua became Jesus in Greek and Latin.
From the Hebrew word simcha, 'joy, gladness', which in Jewish life also means a happy occasion such as a wedding. A traditional name in Ashkenazi communities, mostly for boys.

assoc.t: simcha, Hebrew and Yiddish for a joyous celebration

e.etymology: From Arabic asad, 'lion'. Asad Allah, 'lion of God', is an honorific of Ali, the Prophet Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law.

assoc.t: Bashar al-Assad, ousted Syrian ruler (same word)

e.etymology: From Arabic adhra, 'virgin, maiden', a title of Mary in Islam. It is common in Turkey, Bosnia and Pakistan, and in the US its sound sits close to Ezra.
A rare name brought to notice in 2018 by singer Zhavia Ward of the TV contest The Four. It is close to Xavia and Zavia, feminine forms of Xavier.
A phonetic American spelling of the sound EYE-luh, usually standing for Isla, the name taken from the Scottish island of Islay, or for Ila.

e.meaning: from an English place name: eel farm or Ella's town
e.etymology: From an English surname taken from several villages called Elton. The names have different Old English sources, among them el, 'eel', or the personal name Ella, plus tun, 'farm, settlement'.
A spelling of Riley, from an English surname and place name, Old English ryge, 'rye', plus leah, 'clearing'. Riley is also an anglicized form of the Irish surname Reilly.
A respelling of Lennox, a Scottish surname and earldom named for the district of Lennox near Loch Lomond, from Gaelic leamhan, 'elm'.
A modern name used in Spanish-speaking families, especially from the Caribbean. Its source is not documented.
American use follows Princess Cirilla, called Ciri, of The Witcher books, games and Netflix series. The name matches an older feminine form of Cyril, from Greek Kyrillos, 'lordly'.

assoc.t: Ciri, Princess Cirilla of The Witcher

e.etymology: A pet form of Euphemia, from Greek eu, 'well', and pheme, 'speech'. It was common as a name in its own right in the 19th century, above all in Scotland.
namesakes: Effie Trinket (the Capitol escort in The Hunger Games)
Effie White (the lead singer in Dreamgirls)

assoc.t: Effie Trinket of The Hunger Games

e.etymology: From the English surname Starr, which comes from the word star. As a first name it is a spelling of Star.
namesakes: Starr Carter (heroine of The Hate U Give)

e.etymology: A spelling close to Kian and Cian that peaked after grooming expert Kyan Douglas appeared on Queer Eye in 2003. Cian is Irish for 'ancient'; Kian is also a Persian name meaning 'king'.
namesakes: Kyan Douglas (grooming expert on the original Queer Eye)

e.etymology: From Persian shayan, 'worthy, deserving, fitting'. It is used in Iran and among Muslim families across South Asia.
From Sanskrit akshara, 'imperishable', from a-, 'not', and kshara, 'perishable'. The same word means a syllable or letter of the alphabet, seen as the lasting unit of speech.
Used as a form of Soraya, the Persian name from Arabic thurayya, the Pleiades, and also as an elaboration of Sara or Sarai. English wrestler Saraya, once WWE's Paige, bears it as her given name.
namesakes: Saraya (English pro wrestler, formerly Paige in WWE)
